blocks.text: Quick verdict

ProxyEmpire is the better value for most users: its entry rate ($3.50/GB) is slightly lower than Infatica's $4/GB, its prepaid traffic never expires, and its $1.97 trial covers residential and mobile. Infatica is the better choice when ZIP-level targeting is essential, for example local SERP or retail pricing checks, when you need IPv6 residential IPs, or when procurement wants ISO certifications and a no-reselling policy in writing. Both are credible mid-market networks; pick on features rather than size.

ProxyEmpire and Infatica are both mid-sized residential networks with roughly 30-40 million advertised IPs and similar entry prices. Where they differ is in what they include. ProxyEmpire includes ISP targeting, rolls over every prepaid gigabyte and sells mobile proxies on the same system. Infatica includes ZIP targeting on every plan, offers a rare IPv6 residential pool and leans heavily on its ethical-sourcing credentials. This comparison looks at which of those features matters for your work.

blocks.text: ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire is a Bulgarian-registered provider (SWIFT SAAS LTD) that has been selling since 2020. Its residential and mobile networks share one system with 30M+ advertised IPs in 170+ countries, and country, region, city and ISP targeting are included at no extra cost. The standout policy is bandwidth rollover: prepaid traffic carries forward indefinitely, even after a subscription lapses. Proxyway's 2026 market tests found ProxyEmpire's pool was the third largest among the providers it tested.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: ProxyEmpire vs Infatica

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $35 with ProxyEmpire and $40 with Infatica: a 12% saving in ProxyEmpire's favour. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; Infatica comes to about $360. The sticker price is only half of it. ProxyEmpire's unused traffic carries forward, while Infatica's does not (subscription traffic resets monthly), so if your usage swings from month to month ProxyEmpire can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

On paper the two networks are similar in size: ProxyEmpire advertises 30M+ residential IPs and Infatica advertises 35M-40M. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, ProxyEmpire lists 170+ countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default), while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With ProxyEmpire: stable connections and traffic that never expires. With Infatica: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests. Run the same small test on both before committing.
SERP and rank tracking: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: ZIP targeting helps local search results. How ProxyEmpire compares: Google was its weakest target in independent tests.

Social media and multi-account management: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions. The limitation on the Infatica side: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. ProxyEmpire: free city and ISP targeting. Infatica: ZIP-level targeting for local prices. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Ad verification and geo-testing: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. ProxyEmpire: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost. Infatica: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Tight budgets: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted. The limitation on the Infatica side: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test ProxyEmpire and Infatica before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle ProxyEmpire vs Infatica faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.

3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country. 4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, ProxyEmpire comes out ahead in 2, Infatica in 1, and 3 are ties. That makes ProxyEmpire the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
